title: Mobility, moving and handling, falls and VTE
blurb: Assess and reduce falls risk to NICE NG249, move people safely with the right equipment, respond to a fall and prevent VTE.
question: Mrs Hamid, 84, is admitted to an older people's ward after a fall at home. A colleague suggests scoring her on a falls risk prediction tool to decide whether she needs a falls assessment. What should the nurse do?

teach.h: Falls: assess the person, not a score
teach.body: A fall is an unexpected event in which a person comes to rest on the ground, floor or a lower level. NICE NG249 (April 2025, replacing CG161) says: do not use falls risk prediction tools to predict a person's risk of falling. Instead, offer people in hospital and residential care (aged 65 or over, or 50 to 64 with a risk factor) a comprehensive, multifactorial falls assessment and act on each risk factor found. In plain English: find out why this person might fall, then fix those reasons.

teach.h: What a comprehensive falls assessment covers (NG249)
head: Area
Includes
rows: Gait, balance, strength, footwear and feet
Continence, dizziness, alcohol, osteoporosis risk, diet and fluids
teach.caption: Community: offer a comprehensive assessment to people who fell in the last year and have frailty, an injury needing treatment, loss of consciousness, could not get up, or 2 or more falls.

teach.body: NG249 says not to use a prediction tool, and as an older inpatient Mrs Hamid should be offered a comprehensive falls assessment anyway. The nurse checks lying and standing BP, screens for delirium, looks at her medicines, vision, continence, footwear and walking, and starts actions: call bell and bed controls explained, walking aid within reach, well-fitting shoes, a toileting plan and a medication review request. She records the plan and shares it at handover.

steps.sub: ABCDE, head injury, hip or spine pain, deformity

steps.sub: Prompt medical assessment, including for head injury

teach.caption: NICE QS86 (as audited by the National Audit of Inpatient Falls): check for injury before moving, use safe manual handling (flat lifting equipment where indicated) and arrange prompt medical assessment.

Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992 (HSE): there are no legal weight limits. LOLER 1998: equipment for lifting people, including hoists and slings, needs a thorough examination at least every 6 months.
MHRA Bed rails guidance (2023): bed rails need an individual risk assessment; gaps can cause entrapment and a person who climbs over rails can fall from a greater height.

root.label: Admission to hospital
root.sub: Assess VTE and bleeding risk as soon as possible, or by first consultant review

children.label: Check contraindications
children.sub: PAD, neuropathy, fragile skin, severe oedema, poor fit

children.label: Measure, fit, monitor
children.sub: Remove daily; check skin 2–3 times a day if mobility is significantly reduced

teach.caption: NICE NG89 recs 1.1.1–1.1.5 and 1.3.1–1.3.7. Encourage mobilisation and hydration; give information on prophylaxis at discharge.

teach.text: Two outdated habits: scoring people on a falls risk tool and stopping there (NG249 says not to use them to predict falls), and lifting a person off the floor straight away after a fall. Check for injury first; suspected hip or spinal injury means flat lifting equipment, not a hoist sling or helping them up.

items: No falls risk prediction tools (NG249); comprehensive multifactorial assessment for older inpatients.
Assessment includes lying and standing BP, cognition and delirium, medicines, vision, continence, gait, footwear.
After a fall: check for injury before moving; flat lifting for suspected hip or spinal injury; prompt medical review.
Manual handling: avoid, assess, reduce; no legal weight limits; hoists and slings examined 6-monthly (LOLER).
VTE: assess on admission; stockings not for PAD, neuropathy, fragile skin; remove daily and check skin.

summary: You can now apply NICE NG249 to falls assessment and prevention, respond safely after an inpatient fall, choose moving and handling approaches in line with HSE regulations, and use NICE NG89 to assess VTE risk and apply anti-embolism stockings safely.

A.q: Mrs Hamid, 84, is admitted to an older people's ward after a fall at home. A colleague suggests completing a falls risk prediction score to decide whether she needs a falls assessment. What should the nurse do?
options: Complete the score and assess her if it is high
Offer a comprehensive falls assessment and plan
Wait for a physiotherapy review before any plan
Use the score instead of a medication review
A.why: NICE NG249: do not use falls risk prediction tools to predict risk; offer inpatients aged 65 or over a comprehensive falls assessment and management.

whyNot.0: NG249 advises against using prediction tools to decide risk.
whyNot.2: Assessment and immediate actions should not wait for one professional.
whyNot.3: Medication review is part of the assessment, not replaced by a score.

A.q: As part of a multifactorial falls assessment for Mr Price, 79, which cardiovascular check does NICE NG249 include?
options: A 24-hour ECG recording
A resting echocardiogram
Lying and standing BP
A peak expiratory flow
A.why: NG249 rec 1.2.2: cardiovascular examination including a lying and standing blood pressure test.

whyNot.0: A 24-hour tape may follow if indicated but is not the named check.
whyNot.1: An echocardiogram is not part of the standard assessment.
whyNot.3: Peak flow measures airflow, not cardiovascular causes of falls.

A.q: Mr Holt, 70, has had a stroke and cannot bear weight. He needs to move from bed to chair. Which approach is safest?
options: A hoist with an assessed sling
Two staff lifting him under his arms
A standing aid with him pulling up
One nurse using a pivot transfer
A.why: MHOR: avoid hazardous manual handling and reduce risk with equipment. A person who cannot weight-bear needs a hoist with an assessed sling.

whyNot.1: Lifting under the arms is hazardous for him and staff.
whyNot.2: A standing aid needs the ability to bear weight.
whyNot.3: A pivot transfer needs weight-bearing and risks a fall.

B.q: Mrs Ivy, 82, has fallen on the ward and is on the floor. She is alert, says her hip hurts and her right leg looks shortened and externally rotated. What should the nurse do?
options: Help her up into a chair with two staff so she is more comfortable
Use the standard hoist sling to lift her straight back to bed
Keep her still, get her reviewed and use flat lifting equipment
Ask her to try standing to see whether she can bear weight
B.why: A shortened, externally rotated leg suggests hip fracture. Check for injury before moving, keep her still, get a prompt medical review and use flat lifting equipment (NICE QS86).

whyNot.0: Lifting her into a chair risks further injury and pain.
whyNot.1: A standard sling flexes the hip; flat lifting is needed for suspected fracture.
whyNot.3: Testing weight-bearing could displace a fracture.

B.q: According to NICE NG89, which person should not be offered anti-embolism stockings?
options: A person with a body mass index of 32 kg/m²
A person who has had a total hip replacement
A person aged 85 who has fallen before
A person with peripheral arterial disease
B.why: NG89 rec 1.3.1: do not offer anti-embolism stockings to people with suspected or proven peripheral arterial disease.

whyNot.0: Obesity alone is not a contraindication, though fit must be checked.
whyNot.1: Surgery increases VTE risk; it is not a contraindication.
whyNot.2: Age alone is not a contraindication.

B.q: Mrs Lewis, 87, is wearing anti-embolism stockings after surgery. She is frail, spends most of the day in bed and has significantly reduced mobility. Under NICE NG89, how often should her skin be inspected?
options: Once a week when stockings are changed
Every 2 hours, day and night
Once daily when washed
2 or 3 times a day, especially heels
B.why: NG89 rec 1.3.7: remove stockings daily for hygiene and skin checks; in people with a significant reduction in mobility, inspect the skin 2 or 3 times a day, particularly over the heels and bony prominences.

whyNot.0: Weekly checks would miss pressure damage.
whyNot.1: 2-hourly is the CG179 skin recheck for non-blanching erythema, not the NG89 stocking interval.
whyNot.2: Daily removal is the minimum for everyone; she needs more frequent checks.

C.q: Mr Allen, 88, has dementia and gets out of bed at night. His son asks for bed rails to stop him falling. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Fit bed rails each night, as his son has requested them
Assess the risks first; rails can harm him if he climbs
Give night sedation so that he stays in bed until morning
Ask staff to keep him in a chair at the nurses' station
C.why: MHRA (2023) bed rails guidance: rails need an individual risk assessment because of entrapment and the risk of falling from a height if the person climbs over. Alternatives (low bed, sensor, toileting plan) may be safer.

whyNot.0: A relative's request does not replace a risk assessment.
whyNot.2: Sedation increases falls and delirium risk.
whyNot.3: Keeping him in a chair restricts his liberty and is not a falls plan.

C.q: Mr Hughes, 76, is an inpatient. His lying BP is 136/80 mmHg and after 3 minutes standing it is 112/70 mmHg; he feels dizzy. He takes several antihypertensives. What should the nurse do next?
options: Record it and repeat the readings in a week
Advise him to stay in bed until he feels better
Report the drop and request a medication review
Give him a glass of water and recheck in an hour
C.why: A symptomatic postural drop is a falls risk factor found by lying and standing BP; NG249 asks for risk factors to be acted on, including a structured medication review.

whyNot.0: Waiting a week leaves a known risk unaddressed.
whyNot.1: Bed rest causes deconditioning; NG249 encourages staying active.
whyNot.3: Fluids may help but the medicines need review by the prescriber.

C.q: A healthcare support worker asks the nurse what the maximum weight is that staff may legally lift. What is the correct answer?
options: No legal limit; avoid, assess and reduce the risk
25 kg for men and 16 kg for women by law
20 kg for any staff member, carried close to the body
Half the staff member's body weight in any situation
C.why: HSE: the Manual Handling Operations Regulations set no specific weight limits; employers must avoid hazardous handling, assess what cannot be avoided and reduce the risk.

whyNot.1: The regulations set no specific weight limits; figures like these are not law.
whyNot.2: There is no legal 20 kg limit.
whyNot.3: No regulation sets a body-weight fraction.

reteach.title: Why do people fall?
reteach.question: If you asked ten older people why they fell, how many different answers might you get?

blocks.body: One person fell because their blood pressure dropped when they stood. Another tripped in loose slippers. Another was confused by an infection, another rushing to the toilet, another dizzy from new tablets. A risk score cannot tell you which; a comprehensive assessment can. That is why NG249 asks for assessment of each factor and an action for each one found.

blocks.text: Keeping people in bed to stop them falling backfires: NG249 encourages people in hospital to get up, dress and walk, because deconditioning increases falls.

explain.body: NG249 rec 1.1.1: do not use falls risk prediction tools to predict risk. Offer comprehensive falls assessment and management to hospital inpatients and residential care residents aged 65 or over (or 50–64 at higher risk).

test.q: What does NICE NG249 say about falls risk prediction tools?
options: Use one on every admission to the ward
Use one weekly for inpatients
Do not use them to predict falls
Use one if aged over 80
test.why: NG249 rec 1.1.1: do not use falls risk prediction tools to predict a person's risk of falling.

whyNot.0: NG249 advises against using them to predict risk.
whyNot.3: Age does not change the recommendation.

explain.body: Stay with the person and call for help. Check for injury before moving (ABCDE, head, hip, spine). Suspected hip or spinal injury: keep still and use flat lifting equipment. Arrange prompt medical review, report and update the plan.

test.q: What is the first step after finding a patient on the floor?
options: Check them for injury
Help them up quickly
Fetch the hoist
Complete an incident form
test.why: Check for injury before moving the person (NICE QS86).

whyNot.1: Moving before checking risks worsening an injury.
whyNot.2: Equipment choice depends on the injury check.
whyNot.3: Reporting follows care, not before it.

explain.body: MHOR: avoid hazardous manual handling, assess what cannot be avoided, reduce the risk. No legal weight limits. LOLER: lifting equipment for people, including slings, thoroughly examined at least every 6 months.

test.q: Under LOLER, how often must a patient hoist and its slings be thoroughly examined?
options: Every 12 months
Every 6 months
Every 3 years
Before each use
test.why: LOLER: equipment for lifting people and all lifting accessories need thorough examination at least every 6 months.

whyNot.0: 12 months applies to other lifting equipment, not people-lifting.
whyNot.3: Pre-use checks are visual; thorough examination is 6-monthly.

explain.body: Assess VTE and bleeding risk as soon as possible after admission or by first consultant review; reassess with change. No stockings with PAD, bypass grafts, neuropathy, fragile skin, dermatitis, gangrene, recent graft, allergy, severe oedema, poor fit. Remove daily; check skin 2–3 times daily if mobility is significantly reduced (NG89 1.3.7).

test.q: When should an inpatient's VTE risk first be assessed under NICE NG89?
options: Within 72 hours of admission to the ward
On the day of discharge, before they go home
After the first 3 days, if still immobile
By the first consultant review at the latest
test.why: NG89: assess VTE and bleeding risk as soon as possible after admission or by the time of the first consultant review.

whyNot.0: Waiting up to 72 hours is later than NG89 advises.
whyNot.1: Discharge is too late for inpatient prophylaxis.
whyNot.2: Waiting 3 days delays prophylaxis; assessment does not wait for immobility.
